subject: Chemistry
title: Why Eggs Solidify When Cooked
description: A 60-second lesson on Why Eggs Solidify When Cooked.

hook.text: A raw egg is liquid protein. Heat it and the proteins unravel and tangle together, turning it solid.

buildup.text: Egg white contains albumin proteins folded into tight balls held together by weak hydrogen bonds.

discovery.text: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds. The proteins unfold (denature) and form new bonds with each other, creating a solid network.

twist.text: This process is irreversible. You can't uncook an egg because the new protein bonds are stronger than the original ones.

climax.text: Egg whites set at 62°C, yolks at 68°C. This 6-degree gap is why soft-boiled eggs have a runny yolk.

punchline.text: Proteins unfold, tangle, and lock. Liquid becomes solid and can't go back.

quiz.question: Why can't you uncook an egg?
options: The denatured proteins form new, stronger bonds that can't be reversed
The water evaporates permanently from the egg
The heat destroys the egg's DNA

details.summary: Heating eggs causes protein denaturation, where heat energy breaks the weak bonds maintaining the folded protein structure. Unfolded proteins then form new cross-links with neighboring proteins through a process called coagulation, creating a solid network that transforms liquid egg into a firm gel.
details.whyItMatters: Egg protein coagulation is a fundamental culinary technique used in custards, meringues, binding, and coating. Temperature control determines whether you get a creamy custard or a rubbery scramble.
takeaways: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions in egg proteins
Unfolded proteins form new cross-links, creating a solid gel network
Different egg proteins coagulate at different specific temperatures

faq.question: Why do overcooked eggs become rubbery instead of staying soft?
faq.answer: Excessive heat causes more protein cross-links to form, squeezing out water trapped in the gel network. The dehydrated, heavily cross-linked protein matrix becomes dense and tough. Gentle cooking at lower temperatures preserves more water and produces a softer, creamier texture.

faq.question: Why does the green ring form around overcooked hard-boiled egg yolks?
faq.answer: Overcooking releases hydrogen sulfide gas from egg white proteins, which migrates to the yolk surface and reacts with iron in the yolk to form ferrous sulfide. This green-gray compound is harmless but indicates the egg was heated too long or at too high a temperature.
